newsitem.title: USA: Clinton chides critics of his educational testing.
newsitem.headline: Clinton chides critics of his educational testing.

text.p: President Bill Clinton, promoting his drive for voluntary national education standards, on Thursday criticised opponents of the plan and said they were selling the future of schoolchildren "down the drain."

Appealing for broad bipartisan support for providing a quality education, Clinton told a joint session of the North Carolina state legislature that "our No. 1 priority has to be to make America's education No. 1 in the world."
"Education holds the key to our future and politics must stop at the schoolhouse door," Clinton told the lawmakers of North Carolina, a state he lost in the November general election.
He acknowledged the stiff opposition his proposal has generated from critics who insist education should be handled at the local level with no meddling by the federal government.

"I am tired of people telling me that there is some reason we shouldn't have that opportunity given to every American child," Clinton said. "We are not protecting our children by denying them the chance to develop their god-given capacity to measure up."
Clinton said he was "convinced that one of the reasons that we've never done this in America is that we were afraid if the news was bad we wouldn't know what to do about it."

"I think that in so doing we have sold our children short ... when we do not hold them to high standards, because we are afraid that in the beginning they won't meet them, we are selling their futures down the drain," he said.
"We don't want to punish people, we want to lift them up," Clinton argued.
In the fight for support, Clinton on Thursday enlisted the backing of the Defence Department and the state of North Carolina in his fight to establish standardised testing of the nation's youth.

In addition to North Carolina, the Pentagon -- which operates 233 elementary and secondary schools for 115,000 children of U.S. military personnel in 14 countries and six states -- also joined the ranks of those willing to participate in the testing, set to begin in 1999.

Clinton has called for voluntary standardised national tests for fourth grade reading and eighth grade mathematics. Under his plan, the federal government initially would pay the costs of the tests, with the states then picking up the expense.
Participation would be voluntary, but Clinton hopes for the involvement of every state to ensure that all students are meeting basic standards.
The effort has drawn bipartisan support as Clinton tries to build on efforts introduced, but never brought to fruition, by Republican Presidents Ronald Reagan and George Bush.

Gov. Jim Hunt, a Democrat, made North Carolina the third state officially to accept Clinton's challenge to participate in the standardised tests. "We're proud of what we're doing for education in this state," Hunt said in introducing Clinton.

North Carolina joined Maryland and Michigan in publicly committing to Clinton's call for the annual testing. Administration officials said Clinton wanted to visit the state to draw attention to the decision in hopes of encouraging more states to participate.
